voice_event.speaker: gallic
voice_event.text: To us Jesus is the crucified one who seeks the unpitied, and without whom we can do nothing. He was also met in the poor: a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. And we held that he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; those who perish, perish against his will. At the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, took away the debt that could not be paid, and his soul was not left in hell.

Sulpitius did not witness any of this: he met Martin decades later and says he had his information "partly from himself ... and partly from those who had lived with him" (Vita ch. XXV). Roberts's Matt. xxv. 40 cross-reference is editorial apparatus (Registry row 17), not Sulpitius's text. voice_event.speaker: gallic
voice_event.text: At the sixth hour he went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. At the ninth hour he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on: a man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. And he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation.

glosses.plain_meaning: A real, present, and at times visible adversary. Martin saw him in many shapes and spoke to him. Our elders detect him in a thought we are ashamed to disclose.
glosses.quick_meaning: A real and present enemy, sometimes visible. Martin knew him in any shape and spoke to him. Our elders find him in the thought we are ashamed to tell. Never a figure of speech.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern hearer wants to read our devil as psychology - inner conflict, a shadow, a primitive name for illness. That is the one reading we cannot allow. Ours is a named, embodied, sometimes visible adversary who takes the shapes of the old gods, who can be spoken to and even offered mercy, and who quotes Scripture in church.
false_friend: a metaphor for psychological conflict, "the shadow," or social evil
demons as a primitive explanation for illness
Martin's conversations with the devil as legend

The strength is mixed, and named: the two Tours pieces (the cloak vision, the Christ with wounds) are Tier-3-shaped wonders told by one author who was not present; the hours-of-the-passion teaching and the guest received as Christ are Egypt's content as Cassian handed it on (gallic.core.gallic caution 1), not a Gallic argument; the grace sentences are the contested Conference XIII, whose contest this record does not resolve. This world wrote no treatise on the person or work of Christ that this build has read; Cassian's own books against Nestorius are unread (gallic.source.cassian-de-incarnatione).

results.message: What does purity of heart mean?

voice_event.speaker: gallic
voice_event.text: Purity of heart meant the monk's immediate goal short of the kingdom itself - a heart cleared to charity. Among the brethren at Marseilles it was the definite mark at which every fast, vigil, reading and renunciation is aimed, the way an archer fixes his gaze on a target. By it all of these are ranked as aids to perfection and never as perfection itself. The end of the whole monastic life is the kingdom of heaven; purity of heart is the nearer goal that must be reached first. It came to us from the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried their teaching to a bishop's new house in Gaul. At Tours the words were not used, but the thing was there: the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes.

glosses.plain_meaning: In Cassian's Marseilles, the immediate goal of the whole monastic life, as distinct from its end, the kingdom of heaven. It is the "definite mark" at which every fast, vigil, reading and renunciation is aimed, "which is charity." By it all of these are ranked as aids to perfection and never as perfection itself.
glosses.quick_meaning: The monk's immediate goal, short of the kingdom itself: a heart cleared to charity. Every fast and vigil is ranked by it as an aid, and never as the point.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Purity of heart - do you mean chastity, or just being sincere?' - neither: we mean the target itself, a state of undistracted charity and "tranquillity of mind" from which the kingdom is reached and by which every fast and vigil is measured and ranked; chastity is one element within it, and our own conference on chastity is missing from our English text.
false_friend: sexual purity or moral spotlessness
a pure heart as sincerity or good intentions
perfection as flawlessness or perfectionism

glosses.plain_meaning: A monk, for us, is a man who has cut himself off from marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter life in Christ's service. The cut shows in his body and his dwelling. But at Tours a soldier still in the ranks could be "regarded as a monk," and so could a bishop in his see.
glosses.quick_meaning: A man cut off from marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter service of Christ. At Tours even a soldier and a bishop wore the name.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Wasn't a monk by definition cloistered and withdrawn - the opposite of a soldier or a bishop?' - not for us: Martin was called a monk while still under arms and stayed one as bishop of Tours, because the word names a severance from kin, marriage and property kept strictly, not an enclosure, and no written Rule of our own defined him.
false_friend: a cloistered professional religious under a written Rule and an abbot
someone who by definition is not a soldier, not a bishop, and not to be found in a city
medieval monasticism in dress and discipline

glosses.plain_meaning: The act that makes a monk: "nothing but the evidence of the cross and of mortification," by which, as Pinufius says, the monk is dead to the world "and its deeds and desires." In the south's received teaching it has three stages. Giving up one's goods, "of what is not our own," is only the first, and "is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the renunciant."
glosses.quick_meaning: The act that makes a monk - a death to the world of which giving up goods is only the first and easiest stage. And the Church still fetches renunciants for its sees.
glosses.translational_sense: 'So renunciation means giving everything up - poverty, celibacy, leaving society for good?' - that is only the first and easiest of three stages for us, "of what is not our own"; the real renunciation is of what belongs to us, our affections and our will, a death "to this world" that extends what every baptized Christian renounced at the font - and after which the Church still comes to fetch the renunciant to be its bishop.
false_friend: giving things up - poverty, celibacy, "detachment" - as the whole of the monastic act
a heroic once-for-all rejection of society
self-denial for its own sake

glosses.plain_meaning: For us perfection is the summit of a graded ascent, not a state of being without fault. It is the declared subject of the Institutes, "the attainment of the perfect life." It is reached "not ... simply by self-denial ... unless there is that charity," climbed "from this fear to hope, from hope to the love of God." And at the summit we confess it is a thing "we cannot even make the effort to obtain ... without the mercy and inspiration of God."
glosses.quick_meaning: The summit of a graded ascent - fear, then hope, then love - with charity as its substance. Not flawlessness, and never reached without grace.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Perfection - do you mean sinlessness, an impossible standard?' - no: a graded ascent with charity as its substance and love at its top, measured by a goal rather than by faultlessness, whose stages are fear, hope and love, and whose summit is the confession that neither the effort nor the understanding of the effort is one's own; at Tours, simply a word of praise.
false_friend: perfectionism - flawlessness, sinlessness, an impossible standard producing anxiety
the perfect as an elite class
a Pelagian claim to be without sin

glosses.plain_meaning: The office our monks keep being taken into. A monk "carried off," "escorted under guard," "bound to the long-avoided office," who then keeps "the objects and virtues of a monk" in a see. And at the same time our own formation teaching names the desire for that office as vainglory's suggestion and the devil's pretext.
glosses.quick_meaning: The office our monks are seized into and must never seek. Fled, then overtaken; kept with a monk's humility; costing the saint some of his power.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Wasn't becoming a bishop either a promotion or a sell-out for a monk?' - neither, for us: the office was something one was seized into by a crowd, a trick, or a "fillet," it cost the saint his power, our own formation manual named wanting it as vainglory, and inside it a monk kept "the objects and virtues of a monk" - and a bishop's singular teaching still counted for nothing against the consent of the ancients.
false_friend: a bishop as an administrator or prelate
monk and bishop as opposed careers, so that a monk-bishop is either a promotion or a sell-out
Pope as the bishop of Rome only
episcopal election as a formal procedure

glosses.plain_meaning: Where we are, named in two registers. For Cassian, the cold, late province that falls short of Egypt. For Sulpitius, a self-mocking "We are Gauls" - and the boast that Europe has Martin.
glosses.quick_meaning: Where we are. For Cassian, the cold province that receives Egypt's rule and falls short of it. For Sulpitius, "We are Gauls" - a joke about our appetites, and a boast that Egypt has no Martin.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern hearer may hear "France," a national pride, or a Western monasticism that thinks itself original. Our Gallic identity is none of these: self-deprecating in the south, self-mocking and defiant in the north, and never proud in the modern way - a cold province that received Egypt's rule and knew it fell short.

Gallic pride

figures_used.bridge_line: The man who lived among the fathers of Egypt and brought their words home to Gaul in a book - who told no tales of his own houses and no miracles, but wrote down how a question about grace troubled him and his friend at morning service.

confidence.divergence_note: Single-voice for the technical term (Cassian) - the most consequential single-voice term in the lexicon - and framed by Cassian himself as Abbot Moses's teaching received from Egypt; Doc_04 rates the attribution of this content to Gaul as Inferential, resting only on Gallic monks having been formed by it. The bare lemma puritas occurs once in Hilary of Arles's own Latin in a non-technical phrase of praise for Honoratus. Tours has the thing without the word. Conferences XII "On Chastity" is excised from the vendored edition - a gap inside this term's own content, stated rather than filled.

The best-attested cross-node term in the lexicon: Sulpitius (Tours) and Cassian (Marseilles) use it independently, and Gennadius and Salvian corroborate. Vincent of Lerins never uses it of himself in what was read; that absence is stated, not filled. The three-kinds taxonomy (coenobite, anchorite, Sarabaite) is Cassian's alone and is framed by him as Egypt's own account, not Gaul's.

Cross-voice: the word and the act are shared across both nodes and a fourth voice (Salvian, who also uses it of the baptismal renunciation every Christian made at the font); the threefold schema is Cassian's alone and framed as Paphnutius's Egyptian teaching. Tours has the thing counselled and done without the technical term. Pruned from Doc_03's Tier-1 estimate because it does not organize independently of the pattern in which the renunciant returns to the Church as a bishop.

Weighted to Cassian: the technical sense is his and received (Moses, Paphnutius, Chaeremon, Nesteros); Sulpitius uses the word only as ordinary praise, and there is no doctrine of perfection at Tours in what was read. Two coverage limits bear on this term and are not filled: Conf. XXIII ("sinlessness") is unread and Conf. XII "On Chastity" is excised. The Latin perfectio is not attested in the vendored translation.

Documented as an author, a corpus, and a founder: the Institutes (for Castor, before the Conferences), the Conferences in three parts to named Gallic dedicatees (Part II not later than 426 on the vendored edition's own reasoning from Honoratus's title), and Gennadius ch. LXII (ancient text) on the two houses at Marseilles, "one for men and one for women, which are still standing." Contested [CT] is what his Thirteenth Conference meant in relation to Augustine and whether "semi-Pelagian" is fair (Chadwick vs. Casiday, Doc_01 §7) - carried at gallic.term.grace and gallic.term.free-will, not resolved here. The interval between his Egyptian journey and his writing in Gaul is not stated in this world's own documents and is not computed. Three of his texts are absent from the vendored English edition by the translator's own excision (Conf. XII, XXII; Inst. VI - row 11). He never mentions Martin, and no Native voice narrates his reaction to Prosper or Augustine - the controversy he is famous for has no narrative form in any Native voice (Doc_09 §8 item 5). Every locus below read directly at Doc_09.

Cross-voice tension by design, marked [PV]: the Egyptian sources Cassian carries treat the office as a temptation (vainglory's wish for holy orders; the devil's pretext), while the Gallic reception in which Cassian, Sulpitius and Hilary of Arles all write treats monk-to-bishop as the destination. Both valences are ours and must stay audible. Hilary's Latin for Honoratus's capture is Doc_04's rendering of rough OCR (wording Inferential/Thin; presence checked by grep). Mathisen's account of the Lerins episcopal network is thesis-level only, and Lerins's own internal life remains the least-documented institution; this record does not fill that gap. The Sulpitius-Pelagianism charge (Gennadius ch. XIX) is a contested biographical datum, not a contest about this term.

No Author Gravity - both nodes, four voices - but two registers, recorded rather than smoothed: Cassian's cold, later, weaker province that falls short of Egypt (receptive), and Sulpitius's self-mocking "We are Gauls" and boast that Europe has Martin (comparative); Salvian's burning provinces; Gennadius's "the Gaul." Dialogue I.26, the fullest Tours-side statement, is Registry-Excluded and not used. "We Gauls" is not Salvian's phrase in what was read. Cassian's "in this country" / "this province" are the translator's renderings; no Latin lemma sought.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: gallic
voice_event.text: We believed Jesus calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation, because that is how grace meets a man in our own life. Among the brethren at Marseilles the teaching came from the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried it to us: grace goes before the will, works with it, and crowns it; a man cannot ascribe the good to himself, and God does not send rich crops to the idle. The same thing was shown at Tours in the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak. Martin gave it while he was still a catechumen, years before his baptism; that night he saw Christ wearing what he had given away. The Lord sought the unpitied before the man who pitied him had come to believe. And we held that those who perish, perish against his will, not because he willed only some to be saved instead of all. That is the weight behind it: grace shown before faith, in a cloak at a gate.

glosses.plain_meaning: In Cassian's Marseilles, the help of God without which no effort reaches its goal. Grace "always co-operates with our will"; it goes before the will and follows it; it inspires the first desire and crowns the last perseverance. We hold it together, on purpose, with a will that stays free - in a relation "that cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man."
glosses.quick_meaning: God's help, without which no effort reaches its goal - going before the will, working with it, and requiring it. Held on both sides at once, by design.
glosses.translational_sense: 'So were you on the side of grace or of works - were you semi-Pelagians?' - the label is a sixteenth-century coinage that appears in our own texts only in the editors' notes; what we held was help that co-operates, precedes and requires labour, on both sides at once, declared beyond reason's grasp - and a Representative who resolves it either way has left us.
false_friend: a binary of grace alone versus works, Augustine versus Pelagius, on one side of which we must be placed
semi-Pelagian as a settled verdict
grace as a feeling or a favour
abstract theology unrelated to how anyone lived

confidence.divergence_note: Contested-Tradition term, two contest types. Meaning: whether Cassian's "co-operates," "precedes" and "inspires us with a good will to begin with" amount to Augustine's prevenient grace or to the position Prosper's Contra Collatorem attacked - the Chadwick (redating Honoratus so that Conf. XIII answers Augustine) versus Casiday (rejecting the redating; little direct polemic) contest, bound to the contested chronology; Cassian's own text says the beginning comes from God in some places and can arise "from our own efforts" in others (XIII.8, XIII.12). Application: whether "semi-Pelagian," a sixteenth-century coinage present in our files only in the editors' apparatus, fairly describes the Massilian position, and whether Vincent and Lerins held it at all (Heurtley's editorial claim, contested). Cross-voice: our own voice (Cassian), the provoking outsider reporting us (Augustine), and a later insider (Faustus, via Gennadius) do not speak in unison. Tours is silent because its corpus closed before the question was posed - an absence, not a disagreement. Faustus's own De gratia is unread beyond a bounded grep, so the in-window Lerins side cannot be stated in its own words.

Documented as to existence, office, and reputation: Sulpitius's Life, Letters, Dialogues, and Sacred History within or just after Martin's own lifetime, corroborated independently by Gennadius ch. XIX (ancient text: "monk and bishop," "a man famous for signs and wonders and virtues"). Everything narrated of him rests on one author, so every story is Widely Accepted, never Documented, at the narrative level (Doc_01 §2.2's rule that one ancient witness is not multiple independent sources); the two stories whose narrative claim is the wonder itself are Tier 3. The year of his birth, of the cloak, of the discharge, and of the election are not given in the text (the emperor is "Julian Caesar," the monastery's founding "after 371" only in the editorial introduction). His death in 397 is the horizon's own fixed point. Whether Sulpitius's virtus-organized Life is modelled on the Vita Antonii (Stancliffe, row 18, unread) is open and bears on how much of G6 is the north's own literary form, not on any fact about Martin.

Single-voice (Sulpitius, Tours). The historicity of the raised catechumen falls under virtus / power's Reported-Experience Status. Roberts's footnotes on baptismal regeneration are editorial. No Latin lemma sought.

uncited_claims.sentence: That is the weight behind it: grace shown before faith, in a cloak at a gate.

named_claim_flags.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles the teaching came from the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried it to us: grace goes before the will, works with it, and crowns it; a man cannot ascribe the good to himself, and God does not send rich crops to the idle.

results.message: Tell me about someone who lived this out.

voice_event.speaker: gallic
voice_event.text: Martin lived this out. He left Caesar's service at a donative, saying I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight. Some bystanders at a city gate laughed at him walking in half a cloak. Bishops at his election said his person was despicable, his clothing mean, his hair disgusting. A presbyter he had raised from boyhood stormed into the courtyard and called his visions ridiculous fancies. At Treves, where bishops had bowed to the emperor's court, in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place; he held it a foul thing that a secular ruler should judge a cause of the Church. He yielded there once to save lives, and never sat with bishops again. He died refusing straw for his bed, rather than set his disciples a softer example.

glosses.plain_meaning: The picture that governs a monk's life among us. A man has changed service - from Caesar's army, or from a worldly career - to Christ's. He now stands girded, under oath, in daily combat against the devil and his own faults. The one who slackens is not a failure but a deserter.
glosses.quick_meaning: A man who has changed service, from Caesar's to Christ's, and now fights the devil and his own faults under oath - with the cross, not with weapons.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Isn't "soldier of Christ" just a metaphor - or, worse, the language of holy war?' - for Martin it was a literal change of service, a real discharge before Caesar and a real oath, and it forbade fighting rather than licensing it; the enemy is the devil and one's own faults, and the weapons are the cross, prayer and the cell.
false_friend: spiritual warfare as a private inner metaphor for temptation
the rhetoric of a militant, crusading Christianity
a devotional phrase with no institutional or biographical content

glosses.plain_meaning: At Tours, the highest thing said of Martin - having the apostles' power over death, demons, and emperors. At Marseilles, the perfection of love, and the first Church's common life.
glosses.quick_meaning: At Tours, the highest word for Martin - the apostles' own power, shown by raising the dead and facing an emperor. At Marseilles, the perfection of love, and the common life of the first Church.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern hearer may reach for "apostolic succession" - a doctrine of orders - or for an institutional adjective. Neither is ours. For us "apostolic" means the apostles' own power possessed by a living saint, or the perfection of love the ascent reaches, or the antiquity of the common life.

glosses.plain_meaning: How formation passes from one person to another among us. A disciple is made by watching - and, later, by reading - a named man whose life is held up as the thing to copy. Our books exist to be that example when the man himself is absent.
glosses.quick_meaning: Formation by copying a named man, seen or read - the method of every house we have, and the reason our books are Lives.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Aren't these Lives just legend, and "imitation" just copying?' - for us the Life was written by a man who says he saw, as the thing to be copied in deed and body, and imitation of a named master was the method by which every monk and bishop we produced was made; our literature is Lives and reported conferences rather than treatises for exactly this reason.

a role model freely chosen by the individual and admired from a distance

confidence.divergence_note: Two of the three founding voices use the phrase independently and in opposite registers - literal biography at Tours (Sulpitius), received discipline of dress and sequence at Marseilles (Cassian). Vincent supplies only the antonym ("secular warfare") and is not claimed as a third attesting voice. The Latin miles Christi is not attested in the vendored translation or the bounded Latin grep.

Cross-voice in referent - three voices, three referents: Sulpitius's predicate of Martin (the apostles' power and standing, "deemed powerful and truly apostolical"), Cassian's summit of love and origin of the coenobium, Vincent's See. The referents never argue because they never meet. The northern predicate is single-voice (Sulpitius), and its historicity falls under virtus / power's Reported-Experience Status. Nobody in the south calls a living man "apostolical." No Latin lemma sought.

All three founding voices attest the term at both nodes, with a real difference in medium: a master seen at Tours and in Cassian's Egypt, fathers read at Lerins. What this record does not assert is the historicity of the exemplar's deeds (the eyewitness claims of Sulpitius and Cassian) - that question belongs to virtus / power, which carries Reported-Experience Status, and to the story inventory.

voice_event.speaker: gallic
voice_event.text: That the office came for us whether we wanted it or not, and that we never reconciled what we felt about it. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that vainglory creates a wish for holy orders, and that the devil can push a man toward the priesthood under the pretext of doing good for many people. At Tours Martin was lured from his monastery by a lie, escorted to the city under a kind of guard, and made bishop though some bishops objected to his mean clothes and disgusting hair. After the forced communion at Treves he never attended a synod again for the rest of his life. And on the island Vincent ruled that an ancient council's decrees should be preferred over the rashness of a few, yet held that no rank exempts a lone dissenter. We were taught to suspect in ourselves any wish to rule others, and taught by our stories that the churches would come for us anyway. The thing one must not desire was the thing one would be seized for. We held both at once and never argued it out between our houses: “The few men of rank who survived the destruction asked the emperors for circus games, as the best cure of all for a ruined city. ... Citizens of Trier, do you long for circus games? You have been plundered and captured. You have lived through slaughter and bloodshed, floggings and captivity, and the destruction of your ruined city again and again. What is more pitiful than this stupidity? What is more painful than this folly? I admit I thought you most miserable when you were suffering destruction. But I see that you are more miserable now, when you demand public shows.”

citations.sentence: We held both at once and never argued it out between our houses: “The few men of rank who survived the destruction asked the emperors for circus games, as the best cure of all for a ruined city. ... Citizens of Trier, do you long for circus games? You have been plundered and captured. You have lived through slaughter and bloodshed, floggings and captivity, and the destruction of your ruined city again and again. What is more pitiful than this stupidity? What is more painful than this folly? I admit I thought you most miserable when you were suffering destruction. But I see that you are more miserable now, when you demand public shows.”

glosses.plain_meaning: A monastery, for us, is simply the place where monks dwell. Martin's wooden cell and the caves around it; a bishop's "new monastery" in a province without one; a house "for women" at Marseilles. Coenobium, the word Cassian brings from Egypt, names not the place but the kind of life kept in it. A congregation "governed by the direction of a single Elder."
glosses.quick_meaning: Simply where monks dwell - a wooden cell and caves, or a bishop's new house. The coenobium is the life kept there: one Elder over a congregation.
glosses.translational_sense: 'You mean an abbey - walls, a church, an abbot, a Rule?' - no: for us "monastery" meant nothing more than "the habitation of monks," a wooden hut and hollowed caves or a bishop's new foundation, and since even the false monks had "monasteries," the south reached for coenobium - one elder over a congregation - when it wanted to say what mattered.
false_friend: an abbey or cloister - a walled precinct with a church, a written Rule, an abbot, enclosure, and a charter
convent for the women's version
an institution with a constitution

glosses.plain_meaning: Chiefly the bond of fellowship. To withhold it is the Church's sharpest sanction; to extend it wrongly defiles. Martin's one forced communion cost him power. A monk at fault loses his place at prayer.
glosses.quick_meaning: The bond of fellowship, with real weight. Withheld from bishops who urged the sword; forced once on Martin and paid for in lost power; lost by a monk at fault until he does penance. The sacrament sits inside it.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern hearer thinks first of the eucharistic rite, or of a denominational "communion," or of excommunication as a legal penalty. For us communion is fellowship with spiritual weight - refused to bishops who urged the sword, forced once and paid for in diminished power, lost by a fault and restored by penance on the ground.
false_friend: "communion" as the sacrament only - the eucharist, "taking communion"

glosses.plain_meaning: Two things at once. At Lerins, the ancients' decree that guards the faith, legitimate because it innovates nothing. At Tours, the assembly of bishops that handed heretics to the sword, and that Martin never entered again.
glosses.quick_meaning: For Vincent, the ancients' decree preferred to the rashness of a few, valid because it adds nothing. For Martin, the assembly that handed heretics to the sword, and which he never attended again. Two hearings we never reconciled.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern hearer wants a council to be a constitutional organ with defined authority, or wants Martin's refusal to be a stand against institutions. Neither fits. For Vincent a council is legitimate only because it hands on what it received; for Martin the synod is where bishops urged the sword, and he would not sit there again.
false_friend: "ecumenical council" as a settled constitutional organ with defined authority
synods as church bureaucracy
Martin's refusal as anti-institutionalism

confidence.divergence_note: The word itself is the best-shared place-term in the lexicon (Sulpitius, Cassian, Salvian, Gennadius; both nodes). The coenobium / monastery distinction and the three kinds are single-voice (Cassian) and, by his own framing, Piamun's Egyptian teaching received. Two women's houses are attested (Tours, Marseilles) with no woman's voice from either. Lerins's internal layout is the least-documented house and is not described.

Widely Accepted at the narrative level: one named ancient author writing within Martin's lifetime or immediately after, of a public event in the city he describes, with a named opponent; the bare fact of the episcopate is corroborated by Gennadius ch. XIX ("monk and bishop"). The reading of the psalm as "chosen by Divine ordination" is reported by Sulpitius as what "was believed," and is carried as the crowd's and the author's framing, not as fact. Sulpitius's hostility to the objecting bishops is his own perspective. The election is undated in the text (the vendored volume's editorial introduction places Marmoutier's founding "after 371"). Roberts's footnotes - on popular election, on Halm's "cogitabat," and on "defensor" in the Vulgate of Ps. viii. 3 - are editorial; the claim that the psalm's Latin word gave the objecting bishop's own name is withdrawn as Roberts's, not Sulpitius's. Every quoted phrase read at npnf211 div ii.ii.x, and the ch. X sequel at div ii.ii.xi, at Doc_09 construction.

elements.surface: At Tours Martin was lured from his monastery by a lie, escorted to the city under a kind of guard, and made bishop though some bishops objected to his mean clothes and disgusting hair.

confidence.divergence_note: No Author Gravity - all three founding voices, both nodes: ecclesial fellowship with consequences in the saint's body at Tours; suspension from prayer at Marseilles; "the unity of communion and of the faith" at Lerins. The one thing this term cannot state from a Native text as read is the sacrament's frequency in Gaul: Gibson's footnote claiming daily communion in Gaul cites a chapter of the book his own edition omits entirely (Inst. VI.viii) - an editor's claim resting on an unread Latin text, carried as editorial and Inferential/Thin, not as our own statement. Latin communionis is attested only in Heurtley's editorial appendix.

Cross-voice tension, directly opposed [PV]: the same institution is the guarantor of truth in Vincent's Lerins (an ancient General Council's decrees preferred to "the rashness and ignorance of a few"; Ephesus, which "innovated nothing") and the thing the saint flees in Sulpitius's Tours (the assembly of bishops that handed the Priscillianists to the sword; "never again did he attend a synod"). The divergence is the finding, not a defect, and the two hearings are never reconciled. Cassian has no council in what was read. No Latin lemma sought.

Widely Accepted at the narrative level: one named, socially located author, in two of his own works - not two converging accounts of one event. Sacred History II.50 narrates an earlier phase (Martin's plea at Treves before Priscillian's execution); Dialogues III.11-13 narrates a later visit after the execution, with the coerced communion, Felix's ordination, and the angel; the two share an author, a setting, and a principle. Contested for the angel's speech and for the diminution of power, which are Martin's own reported experience ("he at once confessed to us with tears") as Sulpitius transmits it through Gallus. Sulpitius's hostile characterization of Ithacius ("no worth or holiness about him," SH II.50) is his own perspective. Registry row 6 (Sacred History) is rated B on a "narrative text not read" session note; II.50 was read directly at Doc_04 and re-read at Doc_09 - a fresh verification the source record's own state does not yet reflect. The text gives no year; Gallus says only that Martin "lived sixteen years after this." Roberts's note on the corrupt text at "Andethanna" is editorial. Every quoted phrase read at npnf211 divs ii.iv.iii.xi-xiii and ii.vi.ii.l at Doc_09 construction.

elements.surface: After the forced communion at Treves he never attended a synod again for the rest of his life.

confidence.divergence_note: Documented as an author and a date: the Commonitory dates itself three years after the Council of Ephesus, to 434 (Doc_01 §2.3), and Gennadius ch. LXV (ancient text) records the work, the pseudonym, and the theft of "the greater part of the second book." Widely Accepted for the attribution to Vincentius. Contested whether he held or only sympathized with the Massilian position (Doc_02 §1); whether "Peregrinus" conceals anything is not settled by any Native text. His death is placed "before 450, and probably shortly after 434" on Gennadius's regnal formula (Doc_01 §2.4); his entry to Lerins is undated - "c. 425" is Inferential-Thin, a floating convention (Doc_01 §2.3) - and the claim that he was brother to Lupus of Troyes is Inferential-Thin and uncorroborated by Gennadius. Of the island he says only that he dwells "in the seclusion of a Monastery." Salvian (row 43) is not licensed for grace-related material and is not drawn on for him.

Widely Accepted: Salvian's own direct address to the city, in the same section (VI.15) as the unburied-dead material. The petitioners are named only as "the few men of rank who had survived destruction" - the story's own actors are the city's remaining elite, not its ordinary population, and this record does not extend the claim beyond that (the host record's own divergence_note draws the same line against gallic.term.church-or-circus's broader, different claim). The moral verdict is Salvian's own framing, carried as his.

Both valences are ours and must stay audible. Hilary's Latin for Honoratus's capture is Doc_04's rendering of rough OCR (wording Inferential/Thin; presence checked by grep). Mathisen's account of the Lerins episcopal network is thesis-level only, and Lerins's own internal life remains the least-documented institution; this record does not fill that gap. The Sulpitius-Pelagianism charge (Gennadius ch. XIX) is a contested biographical datum, not a contest about this term.

The reading of the psalm as "chosen by Divine ordination" is reported by Sulpitius as what "was believed," and is carried as the crowd's and the author's framing, not as fact. Sulpitius's hostility to the objecting bishops is his own perspective. The election is undated in the text (the vendored volume's editorial introduction places Marmoutier's founding "after 371"). Roberts's footnotes - on popular election, on Halm's "cogitabat," and on "defensor" in the Vulgate of Ps. viii. 3 - are editorial; the claim that the psalm's Latin word gave the objecting bishop's own name is withdrawn as Roberts's, not Sulpitius's. confidence.divergence_note: Widely Accepted at the narrative level: one named, socially located author, in two of his own works - not two converging accounts of one event. Sacred History II.50 narrates an earlier phase (Martin's plea at Treves before Priscillian's execution); Dialogues III.11-13 narrates a later visit after the execution, with the coerced communion, Felix's ordination, and the angel; the two share an author, a setting, and a principle. Contested for the angel's speech and for the diminution of power, which are Martin's own reported experience ("he at once confessed to us with tears") as Sulpitius transmits it through Gallus. Sulpitius's hostile characterization of Ithacius ("no worth or holiness about him," SH II.50) is his own perspective. Registry row 6 (Sacred History) is rated B on a "narrative text not read" session note; II.50 was read directly at Doc_04 and re-read at Doc_09 - a fresh verification the source record's own state does not yet reflect. The text gives no year; Gallus says only that Martin "lived sixteen years after this." Roberts's note on the corrupt text at "Andethanna" is editorial. references.spoken_rendering: The few men of rank who survived the destruction asked the emperors for circus games, as the best cure of all for a ruined city. ... Citizens of Trier, do you long for circus games? You have been plundered and captured. You have lived through slaughter and bloodshed, floggings and captivity, and the destruction of your ruined city again and again. What is more pitiful than this stupidity? What is more painful than this folly? I admit I thought you most miserable when you were suffering destruction. But I see that you are more miserable now, when you demand public shows.
references.speaker: Salvian of Marseilles

confidence.divergence_note: Widely Accepted: Salvian's own direct address to the city, in the same section (VI.15) as the unburied-dead material. The petitioners are named only as "the few men of rank who had survived destruction" - the story's own actors are the city's remaining elite, not its ordinary population, and this record does not extend the claim beyond that (the host record's own divergence_note draws the same line against gallic.term.church-or-circus's broader, different claim). The moral verdict is Salvian's own framing, carried as his.

confidence.divergence_note: Cross-voice tension by design, marked [PV]: the Egyptian sources Cassian carries treat the office as a temptation (vainglory's wish for holy orders; the devil's pretext), while the Gallic reception in which Cassian, Sulpitius and Hilary of Arles all write treats monk-to-bishop as the destination. Both valences are ours and must stay audible. Hilary's Latin for Honoratus's capture is Doc_04's rendering of rough OCR (wording Inferential/Thin; presence checked by grep). Mathisen's account of the Lerins episcopal network is thesis-level only, and Lerins's own internal life remains the least-documented institution; this record does not fill that gap. The Sulpitius-Pelagianism charge (Gennadius ch. XIX) is a contested biographical datum, not a contest about this term.

end_references.label: The office as temptation and destiny inside the house
